name: glinski hexagonal chess
description: Glinski-style hexagonal chess on a 91-cell hexagon, with promotion on the far edge. Every cell has six neighbours. A rook slides through the six edge neighbours, a bishop through the six cells that touch two of them, a queen does both, a king steps one cell in any of those twelve directions, and a knight leaps to the twelve nearest cells no rook or bishop line reaches. A pawn steps straight forward, two on its first move, and takes on the two neighbours either side of forward. A pawn that reaches the far edge, the eleven cells from which it has no step forward, becomes a queen, rook, bishop or knight. There is no en passant and no castling. Each side has a king, a queen, two rooks, two knights, three bishops and nine pawns in a wedge. The second army is the first turned half a turn, so each king faces the other queen and each side promotes on the cells the other army started from. Checkmate wins; stalemate is a draw.

provenance.source: docs/game-ideas.md, Q281 specified: a native hexagon
provenance.history: Schema 16's showcase for board.shape (Q281a4): hex-glinski-promoting with board.shape "hexagon" and its rules.obstacles removed, and nothing else. It compiles to the parent's tables array by array, so it demonstrates by identity, as board.lattice did in schema 14: its measured score is predicted to equal the parent's to the last printed digit under the same basis.
